meta.title: The Blueprint Press
meta.tagline: a language model reads a repo, writes one JSON file, and a fixed renderer prints the drawing

groups.label: The authoring pass
groups.note: the only part a model performs

groups.label: The contract
groups.note: what the two halves agree on

groups.label: The drawing
groups.note: runs in the browser, every frame

nodes.label: Repo survey
nodes.summary: reads the manifest, the entrypoints and the directory tree before deciding anything
nodes.detail: The first phase of PROMPT.md. It reads package.json / Cargo.toml / pyproject, finds the binaries and servers, and walks the tree two levels deep. Nothing is written during this pass — its only job is to stop the model from inventing an architecture before it has seen one.

nodes.label: Node census
nodes.summary: turns directories and modules into 15-40 subsystems, not files
nodes.detail: Collapses the tree into the units a reader would actually name out loud. Leaf modules get folded into their parent and mentioned in that parent's detail text instead of becoming their own block. The 15-40 band is enforced as a warning by the validator, because under 15 the drawing is trivial and over 40 it turns to soup.

nodes.label: Edge tracing
nodes.summary: finds real calls, channels, tables and routes — and deletes the rest
nodes.detail: Every connection has to name something concrete in its payload field: a type signature, a function, an SQL table, an HTTP route. The rule is deliberately harsh — if the model cannot name what crosses a line, the line is not real and gets dropped. This is what keeps the diagram from degenerating into boxes joined by vibes.

nodes.label: Narrative draft
nodes.summary: writes the right-hand panel in plain English and links phrases back to blocks
nodes.detail: Produces the WHAT IT DOES and HOW IT'S BUILT tabs as typed blocks rather than HTML, so the panel can never break the layout. Phrases wrapped in double brackets become live references: hovering one lights up the matching block in the drawing, and hovering the block lights up every phrase pointing at it.

nodes.label: Authoring model
nodes.summary: the language model running the six phases against a checked-out repo
nodes.detail: Any model with file-reading tools and enough context to hold a repo survey. It never touches the renderer, the stylesheet, or the build script — its entire output surface is one JSON document. That restriction is the whole reason results are reproducible instead of a new invention every run.

nodes.label: codeviz.json
nodes.summary: the single hand-authored artifact: meta, stats, groups, nodes, edges, narrative
nodes.detail: Six top-level keys and nothing else. This file is the entire interface between the model and the drawing, which means it is also the thing you edit by hand when the model gets a detail wrong. Re-running the build after a manual edit takes under a second.

nodes.label: JSON Schema
nodes.summary: draft 2020-12 definition of every field, enum and length limit
nodes.detail: Machine-readable and strict: additionalProperties is false everywhere, so a typo'd field name is an error rather than silently ignored data. Field descriptions double as authoring guidance, which is why they read like instructions instead of documentation.

nodes.label: Validator
nodes.summary: checks structure, cross-references and prose quality with zero dependencies
nodes.detail: Re-implements the schema by hand so it can also check the things JSON Schema cannot express: that every edge endpoint resolves, that every bracketed narrative reference points at a real node, that no node is left unwired. Errors block the build; warnings — vague payloads, single-sentence details, marketing language in the tagline — print and let it through.

nodes.label: Kind table
nodes.summary: the fixed map from node kind to footprint, height and hatching
nodes.detail: Eight node kinds and six edge kinds, closed sets. Because the mapping is a table rather than a model decision, a store always reads as a laminated slab and a queue always reads as a ribbed stack — across every repo, forever. The visual grammar stays learnable.

nodes.label: build.mjs
nodes.summary: one command that validates, inlines and writes the finished file
nodes.detail: Takes a codeviz.json and emits a standalone HTML document. It refuses to build on validation errors unless you pass --force, which exists for the case where you want to look at a half-finished blueprint while you fix it.

nodes.label: Inliner
nodes.summary: splices stylesheet, renderer, three.js and data into one document
nodes.detail: three.js is embedded as a base64 data URL inside an import map, which Chrome and Firefox resolve happily even from file://. That one trick is what removes the need for a dev server, a bundler, or a network connection when someone opens the result.

nodes.label: Vendored three.js
nodes.summary: r169 module build, checked into the repo rather than fetched
nodes.detail: Pinned on purpose. A CDN reference would mean a blueprint you generated last year silently changes behaviour when the CDN moves, and would break entirely on a machine without internet. The cost is about 660 KB in every output file.

nodes.label: Blueprint HTML
nodes.summary: the deliverable: one file, no server, no network, no install
nodes.detail: Roughly a megabyte, most of it three.js. You can email it, drop it in a wiki, or commit it next to the repo it describes. Opening it from disk works because nothing inside it points anywhere outside itself.

nodes.label: Data intake
nodes.summary: parses the embedded JSON and quarantines broken references
nodes.detail: Reads the inline JSON block, checks the protocol version, then filters out nodes with unknown groups or kinds and edges with unresolvable endpoints. Dropped items are collected and logged rather than thrown, so a nearly-correct blueprint still draws and the damage is visible in the console.

nodes.label: Layout engine
nodes.summary: groups become bands, longest-path rank becomes columns, then it recentres
nodes.detail: Each group gets a horizontal band on the floor; inside a band, nodes are ranked by longest path from their sources and stacked to fill the depth. Cycles are handled by bounding the relaxation passes rather than by detecting them. There is no randomness anywhere, so the same JSON always yields the identical arrangement.

nodes.label: Geometry factory
nodes.summary: extrudes each block and gives every visible face its own material
nodes.detail: Box faces get different flat colours to fake the lighting, so the scene needs no lights at all and stays perfectly crisp. Stores are built as several stacked sheets and queues as a row of thin plates, which is what makes those two kinds recognisable at a glance from across the drawing.

nodes.label: Route planner
nodes.summary: orthogonal routes with chamfered corners, anchored to block silhouettes
nodes.detail: Lines leave a block at its edge rather than its centre, take at most one dog-leg, and have their corners cut at forty-five degrees. Each route also gets an invisible fat tube alongside it so a one-pixel hairline is still something you can actually hover.

nodes.label: Packet field
nodes.summary: every travelling dot in one instanced draw call, capped at 900
nodes.detail: Each connection carries one to six packets depending on its declared traffic volume, and all of them live in a single InstancedMesh whose matrices are rewritten each frame. Hovering a line triples its packet speed and switches those instances to the accent colour, which is how you confirm which hairline you are actually reading.

nodes.label: Hatch atlas
nodes.summary: vertical, cross and dot patterns drawn once into canvas textures
nodes.detail: Generated procedurally at startup and cached by pattern name, so nothing ships as an image asset and the output file stays free of binary blobs. The same generator draws the faint floor grid at a larger scale.

nodes.label: Camera rig
nodes.summary: orthographic, locked to true isometric, four rotation snaps only
nodes.detail: The camera sits along the (1,1,1) axis, which is exactly the classic isometric elevation. Free orbit is deliberately not offered — pan, zoom and ninety-degree snaps are the whole control set, because an arbitrary angle is what turns an engineering drawing back into a generic 3D toy.

nodes.label: Pick raycaster
nodes.summary: one ray, blocks tested before lines
nodes.detail: Blocks win ties against connectors, so a line passing under a block never steals the hover. Both hit types resolve to the same shape — a kind and an id — which is why the sidebar, the narrative panel and the drawing can all drive the same highlight state.

nodes.label: Hover card
nodes.summary: the reading surface: summary, detail, source paths, metrics, payload
nodes.detail: For a block it shows what the subsystem does, which files back it, what it is built with and how many connections touch it. For a connector it shows the two endpoints, the concrete payload, and a note on when the path fires and what happens if it fails. The card flips sides near the viewport edge so it never runs off-screen.

nodes.label: Sidebar index
nodes.summary: every block listed under its group, with connection counts
nodes.detail: Hovering a row highlights the block and its neighbours; clicking one flies the camera to it and pins the selection. It is the only way to find a block whose label is currently hidden because you are zoomed out past the label threshold.

nodes.label: Narrative panel
nodes.summary: tabbed prose whose highlighted phrases are wired to the blocks
nodes.detail: Blocks of typed text are rendered rather than raw HTML, and the two inline markups — node references and glossary terms — are the only formatting allowed. Everything else is escaped, so a stray angle bracket in a model's prose cannot break the page.

nodes.label: Frame loop
nodes.summary: eases the camera, advances the packets, repositions the labels
nodes.detail: A single requestAnimationFrame loop that pauses itself when the tab goes to the background. Node labels are HTML rather than 3D text, so they stay crisp at any zoom; the loop projects each block's top point to screen coordinates and moves the divs to match.

edges.label: directory tree
edges.detail: Hands over everything the survey found without interpreting it. The census is the first point where a judgement call gets made, and it can only be as good as this list.

edges.label: entrypoints
edges.payload: bin targets, server mains, exported handlers
edges.detail: Tracing starts from the entrypoints and follows calls outward. Without them the model tends to guess at connections from directory names alone.

edges.label: node ids
edges.payload: the settled set of subsystem ids
edges.detail: Edges cannot be traced until the nodes are fixed, because an edge is only meaningful between two named subsystems. Adding a node later means re-checking every edge that should now terminate on it.

edges.label: runs the census
edges.detail: The model performs each phase in order rather than emitting the JSON in one pass. Skipping ahead is the single most common cause of a blueprint full of plausible but wrong edges.

edges.label: writes the panel
edges.detail: Prose is written last, once the graph is settled, so the narrative can reference real node ids. Writing it first reliably produces references to nodes that never get created.

edges.label: nodes[]
edges.payload: nodes[] with kind, group, summary, detail, paths
edges.detail: Each subsystem becomes one node object. The kind field is chosen from the closed enum, never invented.

edges.label: edges[]
edges.payload: edges[] with from, to, kind, payload, detail
edges.detail: Only connections with a nameable payload survive to this point. The payload string is what a reader sees in the connector hover card, so it is written for a human, not as an internal note.

edges.label: narrative
edges.detail: Prose arrives as typed blocks with two permitted inline markups. Raw HTML is escaped on render, so anything fancier than that simply shows up as literal text.

edges.label: field contract
edges.payload: enums, length limits, required keys, descriptions
edges.detail: The schema's descriptions are written as instructions rather than documentation, so a model reading the schema alone still authors reasonable content. It is included verbatim in the prompt for exactly that reason.

edges.label: shape vocabulary
edges.detail: The model picks a kind knowing what shape it will produce, which lets it reason about how the finished drawing will read. It cannot change the mapping.

edges.label: candidate blueprint
edges.detail: Validation runs before anything is inlined. Catching a dangling edge here costs a second; catching it after delivery costs a round trip with whoever you sent the file to.

edges.label: mirrored rules
edges.payload: enums and limits, hand-copied into validate.mjs
edges.detail: Deliberate duplication: it keeps the validator dependency-free and lets it add cross-reference and prose checks that JSON Schema has no way to express. The cost is that both files have to move together.

edges.label: validate first
edges.detail: Errors abort the build unless --force is passed. Warnings always print and never block, because most of them are style advice rather than breakage.

edges.label: splice
edges.detail: The inliner matches two anchor patterns in the template and refuses to run if either has drifted. That guard exists because a silently half-inlined file looks fine until someone opens it offline.

edges.label: base64 import map
edges.detail: Encoding the library as a data URL inside an import map is what lets the module graph resolve under file://, where a relative module import would be blocked by CORS.

edges.label: embedded data
edges.detail: The document is pretty-printed into a JSON script tag, with any closing-script sequence escaped. That means you can open a built blueprint in an editor and read its data straight out of the file.

edges.label: one file out
edges.payload: ~1 MB HTML with zero external references
edges.detail: This is the only artifact anyone else ever sees. Everything upstream of it is machinery.

edges.label: on load
edges.detail: If the block is missing, unparseable, or still the unfilled placeholder, the renderer shows the no-data panel with the exact reason instead of a blank canvas.

edges.label: clean graph
edges.payload: nodes and edges with every reference resolved
edges.detail: Layout runs exactly once, at startup. Nothing downstream re-positions a block, which is why panning and rotating never rearrange the drawing under you.

edges.label: floor coordinates
edges.detail: Positions are settled before any mesh exists. Manual pos overrides in the JSON are applied here and win over the computed rank.

edges.label: block silhouettes
edges.detail: Routing needs the footprints, not just the centres, so lines can terminate on a block's edge. This is why routes are planned after geometry sizing rather than alongside it.

edges.label: face textures
edges.detail: Three patterns cover all eight node kinds. Side faces are hatched and top faces mostly left plain, which is what gives the blocks their drawn-by-hand read.

edges.label: shape lookup
edges.payload: KIND[node.kind] -> { fp, h, hatch, ribs, slabs }
edges.detail: A single table lookup decides the entire appearance of a block. Weight scales it, but never changes which shape it is.

edges.label: arc-length tables
edges.detail: Precomputing the lengths turns per-frame packet placement into a short walk plus one lerp. Without it, every packet would re-measure its whole route sixty times a second.

edges.label: block targets
edges.detail: Every mesh that makes up a block carries the same node id, so a stacked store with five sheets still resolves to one hover target.

edges.label: line targets
edges.payload: invisible tube meshes tagged with userData.edgeId
edges.detail: The tubes are fully transparent but still visible to the raycaster, which is the trick that makes a hairline hoverable. They are tested only after the blocks miss.

edges.label: hover changed
edges.detail: Fires only on an actual change of target, so the card is not rebuilt on every mouse move. The same event drives the highlight repaint across all three panels.

edges.label: boost
edges.detail: Hovering anything raises the boost flag on the touched connections. The packets on those lines then run about three times faster and switch to the accent colour.

edges.label: synthetic hover
edges.detail: Sidebar rows and narrative references push the same hover state the raycaster would, so the highlight logic has exactly one implementation. Clicking instead pins a selection and moves the camera.

edges.label: phrase hover
edges.detail: This is the link that makes the prose and the drawing feel like one object: read a sentence, and the thing it names lights up beside it.

edges.label: fly to block
edges.detail: Sets the camera's target and a minimum zoom, both of which the frame loop then eases toward. Nothing snaps, so you keep your bearings.

edges.label: ease
edges.payload: lerp of target, zoom and yaw each frame
edges.detail: All camera motion is a goal plus an exponential ease, so competing inputs — a click, a drag, a keypress — blend instead of fighting. Rotation is quantised to ninety degrees before easing.

edges.label: advance
edges.detail: One pass over every packet per frame, writing straight into the instance buffers. The 900-packet cap keeps that pass bounded no matter how busy the graph is.

edges.label: project labels
edges.detail: Labels are HTML divs pushed around by the loop rather than 3D text, so they stay pixel-crisp and can use the real font. Below a zoom threshold they fade out entirely to keep the field readable.

blocks.text: The Blueprint Press

This repository turns a codebase into the drawing you are currently looking at. You point a language model at a repo, it produces a single JSON file, and a fixed renderer prints that file as an animated isometric plan you can hover your way through.

The important design decision is what the model is allowed to write. It does not write HTML, or CSS, or three.js code. It writes [[one JSON document|codeviz_json]] and nothing else. Everything you see — the hatching, the routing, the camera, the panels — is fixed machinery that behaves identically for every repo it is ever pointed at.

That split is why the results are comparable. Two blueprints of two different systems can be read side by side, because a laminated slab means {{store}} in both of them and a ribbed stack means {{queue}} in both of them. Ask a model to free-hand a diagram twice and you get two unrelated visual languages.
How to read the drawing

Blocks are subsystems, not files. Their shape tells you what kind of thing they are; the [[kind table|kind_table]] is closed, so the vocabulary is small enough to learn in about a minute. Height and footprint scale with declared weight, which is the author's way of saying this one matters more.

The hairlines on the floor are real connections. Every one of them names something concrete — a type, a function, a table, a route — which you can read by hovering it. Travelling dots show relative traffic; hovering a line speeds its dots up so you can confirm you are reading the line you think you are.
Hover a block for what it does and which files back it. Hover a line for what actually crosses it. Highlighted phrases in this panel are live — hover one and its block lights up in the drawing.
Making one

Give a model with file access the prompt in PROMPT.md and a checked-out repo. It runs a six-phase pass — [[survey|repo_survey]], [[census|node_census]], [[tracing|edge_tracing]], [[narrative|narrative_draft]], self-check, emit — and hands back a codeviz.json.

node scripts/validate.mjs my-repo.codeviz.json
node scripts/build.mjs   my-repo.codeviz.json
The second command writes [[one self-contained HTML file|blueprint_html]]. No server, no bundler, no network. Open it off disk and it works.
Three parts that barely know each other

The [[authoring pass|authoring_model]] is prose and judgement, performed by a model. The [[contract|json_schema]] is a strict document format with closed enums. The [[drawing|layout_engine]] is a fixed browser renderer. Neither end can reach into the other, and that is the entire architecture.
The contract does the enforcing

Every field has a length limit and every enum is closed, with additionalProperties set to false throughout — so a misspelled key is an error rather than data that silently vanishes. The [[validator|validator]] then re-checks by hand the things a schema cannot see: that both endpoints of every connection resolve, that every bracketed phrase in this panel points at a node that exists, that nothing is left unwired.

It also nags about quality. A payload of just "data" is a warning. A one-sentence hover detail is a warning. Marketing adjectives in the tagline are a warning. None of them block a build; all of them are things that make a blueprint worse to read.
Why it looks like this

The [[camera|camera_rig]] is orthographic and pinned to the (1,1,1) axis — exactly the classic isometric elevation. Free orbit is not offered. Ninety-degree snaps and panning are the whole control set, because the moment you can tumble to an arbitrary angle the thing stops reading as an engineering drawing.

There are no lights in the scene. Faces are flat-coloured to fake the shading, which keeps every edge perfectly crisp at any zoom and makes the render cost trivial. The [[hatching|hatch_atlas]] is drawn procedurally into canvas textures at startup, so the output file carries no image assets.

[[Connections|route_planner]] leave a block at its silhouette rather than its centre, take at most one dog-leg, and have their corners cut at forty-five degrees. Each hairline is shadowed by an invisible fat tube so it can actually be hovered — a one-pixel line is otherwise impossible to hit with a mouse.
Determinism

There is no Math.random and no clock-seeded value anywhere in the renderer. [[Layout|layout_engine]] is a longest-path rank inside per-group bands, with cycles handled by bounding the relaxation passes rather than detecting them. The same JSON always produces the identical arrangement, which means you can re-run a blueprint after editing one node and diff what moved.
Why three.js is checked in

[[The library|three_vendor]] is vendored at r169 and embedded in every output as a base64 data URL inside an import map. That resolves under file://, where a relative module import would be blocked. It costs about 660 KB per file and buys a deliverable that will still render identically on a laptop with no internet in five years.
Everything on this screen was generated from examples/self.codeviz.json, which is the repository describing itself. If something here is wrong, that file is the thing to edit.

glossary.definition: A node kind drawn as a laminated slab: a database, an archive, a filesystem, or any other place data comes to rest.
A node kind drawn as a ribbed stack of thin plates: a channel, a buffer, or a job queue — anything work waits in.
